questions.stem: In the sentence "Her honesty won the admiration of the whole class", the word *honesty* is which class of noun?
questions.explanation: An abstract noun names something you cannot see, touch or weigh — a quality, state, feeling or idea. *Honesty* is a quality of character, so it is abstract. A useful test: if you cannot perceive it with any of the five senses, it is abstract.

distractorRationale.a: Proper nouns name a particular person, place or institution and take a capital letter, such as Enugu or Amina
distractorRationale.c: A collective noun names a group counted as one unit, such as class or team — note that *class* in this sentence is the collective noun, not *honesty*
distractorRationale.d: Material nouns name substances such as gold, sand or cotton

questions.stem: In the sentence "A herd of cattle blocked the road to Lokoja", the word *herd* is which class of noun?
questions.explanation: A collective noun names a group of people, animals or things treated as a single unit. *Herd* names a group of cattle, so it is collective. Other examples are a flock of birds, a swarm of bees and a bunch of bananas.

distractorRationale.a: Abstract nouns name qualities and ideas, which a herd is not — a herd can be seen and counted
distractorRationale.b: Material nouns name substances, not groups
distractorRationale.d: *Lokoja* is the proper noun in this sentence; *herd* is not the name of one particular group

questions.stem: Choose the correct plural form of the noun *criterion*.
questions.explanation: *Criterion* is borrowed from Greek and keeps its Greek plural, *criteria*. The same pattern gives *phenomenon* the plural *phenomena*. Because *criteria* is already plural, saying "one criteria" is an error.

distractorRationale.a: Applies the regular English -s ending to a word that keeps its Greek plural
distractorRationale.b: Adds -s to a form that is already plural, a very common error
distractorRationale.d: Uses an Italian-style ending that English does not borrow for this word

questions.stem: Choose the correct plural form of the compound noun *commander-in-chief*.
questions.explanation: In a compound noun joined by a preposition, the plural marker goes on the head word — the word that names the person or thing. Here the head is *commander*, so it becomes *commanders-in-chief*. The same rule gives *mothers-in-law* and *passers-by*.

distractorRationale.a: Pluralises the last word instead of the head word
distractorRationale.c: Pluralises two words when only the head word takes the marker
distractorRationale.d: Applies the -f to -ves rule, which belongs to words like leaf and thief, not to chief in a compound

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses the noun correctly?

options.text: My uncle gave me two useful advices.
My uncle gave me two pieces of useful advice.
My uncle gave me two advices that were useful.
My uncle gave me two useful advice.

questions.explanation: *Advice* is an uncountable noun, so it has no plural form and cannot follow a number directly. To count it you need a partitive expression such as *a piece of advice* or *two pieces of advice*. The same applies to information, furniture, equipment and luggage.

distractorRationale.a: Adds -s to an uncountable noun
distractorRationale.c: Same error as option a, simply moved into a relative clause
distractorRationale.d: Keeps the number *two* in front of an uncountable noun with no partitive, so the sentence does not agree

questions.stem: In the sentence "The headmaster gave Amina a prize", what is the grammatical function of *Amina*?
questions.explanation: The thing actually handed over is the prize, so *a prize* is the direct object. *Amina* is the person who receives it, which makes her the indirect object. The test is that you can rewrite the sentence as "gave a prize **to Amina**" — anything that can take *to* or *for* in the rewrite is the indirect object.

distractorRationale.a: *The headmaster* performs the action, so the headmaster is the subject
distractorRationale.b: *A prize* is what was given, so that is the direct object
distractorRationale.d: *Gave* is an action verb, not a linking verb, so it takes objects rather than a complement

questions.stem: In the sentence "Chinua Achebe became a celebrated novelist", the phrase *a celebrated novelist* functions as the
questions.explanation: *Became* is a linking verb, and a linking verb does not act on an object; it points back to the subject. *A celebrated novelist* renames Chinua Achebe, so it is a subject complement. Common linking verbs are be, become, seem, appear, remain and turn.

distractorRationale.b: A direct object receives an action, but nothing is being acted upon here — nobody is 'becoming' something else
distractorRationale.c: There is no recipient in the sentence, so there can be no indirect object
distractorRationale.d: The phrase names what Achebe was, not how he did anything

questions.stem: A common noun such as *river* takes a capital letter whenever it appears in the phrase *River Niger*.
questions.explanation: True. When a common noun forms part of the full name of one particular place, it becomes part of a proper noun and takes a capital letter, as in River Niger, Lagos State and Ahmadu Bello University. Written alone in a general sense — "we crossed the river" — it stays lower case.

questions.stem: Write the correct plural form of the compound noun *passer-by*.
questions.explanation: The head word of the compound is *passer*, the person doing the passing, so the plural marker attaches there: *passers-by*. Writing *passer-bys* pluralises the preposition instead of the noun, which English does not allow.

questions.stem: In the sentence "Mr Okoro, our principal, addressed the assembly this morning", the phrase *our principal* is
questions.explanation: A noun phrase placed beside another noun to identify it further, and set off by commas, is said to be in apposition. *Our principal* simply gives extra information about Mr Okoro; remove it and the sentence still stands. The subject remains *Mr Okoro*.

distractorRationale.a: *Mr Okoro* is the subject; the appositive only describes him and could be deleted
distractorRationale.c: *The assembly* is what was addressed, so that is the object
distractorRationale.d: *This morning* is the adverbial in this sentence, and it tells time rather than place

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a proper noun?
questions.explanation: A proper noun is a specific name for a particular person, place, or organization. 'Nigeria' is a specific country, which qualifies it as a proper noun.

distractorRationale.a: A common noun that refers to any city, not a specific one.
distractorRationale.c: An abstract noun that refers to a state of being, not a specific name.
distractorRationale.d: A collective noun referring to a group, but not a specific name.

questions.stem: What is the plural form of the noun *child*?
questions.explanation: The plural form of 'child' is 'children', which is an irregular plural noun. Unlike regular nouns, the plural form does not simply add 's' or 'es'.

distractorRationale.a: Incorrect as 'childs' is not a recognized plural form.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect as 'childes' is not a recognized plural form.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect as 'childer' is not a recognized plural form.
